opus-5.5.text:
I think simulation data is valuable, but its value depends on what you're asking it to do.

Simulation is cheap, scalable, and controllable. You can generate millions of trajectories, randomize lighting, textures, object poses, and physical parameters, and get perfect labels for free: depth, segmentation, contact forces, everything. For things like perception pretraining, locomotion, or learning the coarse structure of a task, sim has proven extremely useful. A lot of the progress in legged locomotion came from training in simulation and transferring to the real robot.

The problem is the sim-to-real gap, and it's not uniform. Rigid-body dynamics and navigation transfer relatively well. But once you get into contact-rich manipulation, like deformable objects, cloth, liquids, or friction-sensitive grasping, the simulators are still not faithful enough. The visual gap is shrinking quickly, especially with neural rendering and generative models, but the physics gap is harder. A policy can learn to exploit artifacts of the simulator that simply don't exist in the real world.

So I assess sim data along a few dimensions. First, does it improve real-world performance when mixed with real data, not just sim benchmarks? That's the only metric that ultimately matters. Second, what's its marginal value? If a small amount of real data plus a large amount of sim beats a larger amount of real data alone, that's a strong signal. Third, diversity. Sim is most useful when it covers situations that are rare, dangerous, or expensive to collect in reality, like edge cases and failure recovery.

My view is that sim won't replace real data, but it's an important part of the data pyramid. At the bottom you have huge amounts of internet video and human data that give broad priors about the world. In the middle you have simulation and synthetic data that provide scale and controllability. At the top you have high-quality real robot data that grounds everything in true physics and embodiment. The best systems will combine all three.

I'm also excited about the convergence of simulation and world models. Instead of hand-building every asset and physics rule, we may increasingly learn simulators from data, generative world models that can produce realistic interactive environments. If that works, the line between "sim data" and "real data" starts to blur, and the question becomes how faithful your world model is, rather than whether the data is simulated.

r001.rationale: The response assesses simulation by its marginal value and diversity, emphasizing coverage of rare situations rather than simply generating large volumes of data.

r002.rationale: It describes simulation as scalable and highlights randomization and diversity; it does not say simulated data can have a narrow, homogeneous distribution.

r003.rationale: It says simulators are not faithful enough for contact-rich manipulation involving deformable objects and identifies the physics gap as difficult.

r004.rationale: It does not mention declining costs of collecting real-robot data for tasks that simulation handles well.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the answer depends on what you mean by "simulation data," because there are really two different things hiding under that word, and they have very different value.

The first kind is traditional physics-engine simulation—you build a scene in something like Isaac or MuJoCo, you put a robot arm in it, and you let it try a task millions of times. The value there is clear: it's cheap, you can get perfect labels, you can reset instantly, and you can randomize everything. For things like locomotion, where the physics is mostly rigid-body contact and the visuals matter less, this has already worked. The quadruped and humanoid walking results we see today are essentially born in simulation.

But for manipulation—which is where most of the economic value is—the picture is much less rosy. The problem is not that we can't render a kitchen. The problem is that we can't simulate the things that actually make manipulation hard: deformable objects, liquids, friction on a greasy surface, a bag of rice that changes shape when you grab it. Every one of those takes an engineer to model by hand, and the long tail is infinite. So you end up with a sim-to-real gap not because the pixels look different, but because the world behaves differently. And the model learns the wrong physics very confidently.

The second kind of "simulation data" is what I've spent most of my time on recently, which is generative models acting as the simulator—what people call world models. Here the idea is reversed: instead of writing physics by hand and rendering it, you learn the dynamics directly from video. The appeal is that the data distribution is the real world's distribution, because it came from real video. You don't have to decide in advance which objects are deformable.

My honest assessment is that this second route is where the long-term value is, but it's not ready to replace real data today. The current models are very good at generating something that looks plausible, and much weaker at being physically consistent over long horizons or in response to specific actions. For a robot policy, "plausible" is not enough. If the cup sometimes passes through the table, the policy learns something wrong. So right now I'd say generative simulation is excellent for augmentation—changing lighting, backgrounds, object textures, making a policy more robust—and for evaluation, where you don't need perfect physics, you just need to catch obvious failures. It is not yet a trustworthy source of the core training signal.

There's one more point I'd make, which is about ratios. People often frame this as sim versus real, and I think that's the wrong framing. The question is: what is the minimum amount of real data you need to anchor the model, and how far can simulated or generated data stretch that anchor? My intuition is that real data will always be the thing that determines the ceiling, and simulation—of either kind—determines how efficiently you reach that ceiling. Real data is the ground truth of what the world does; simulation is a way to interpolate between the ground truth points you've collected. If you have no real anchor, the interpolation drifts. If you have a lot of real data, simulation mostly saves you money.

So if a robotics team asked me today, I'd say: don't bet your foundation on simulation, but also don't ignore it. Collect real data in the environments you actually care about, and use simulation—increasingly, learned simulation—to multiply its coverage. And watch the world model space closely, because the moment those models become action-consistent and physically reliable, the economics of this whole field change.

r002.rationale: It describes limits in modeling manipulation and a long tail of objects, but does not say simulation data can have a narrow, homogeneous distribution.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies deformable objects as difficult to simulate and says each requires an engineer to model by hand.

r004.rationale: It says simulation is cheap and already works for locomotion, but does not state that real-robot data collection costs are declining for those tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think simulation data is valuable, but its value depends on what you want the robot to learn. For perception and basic spatial reasoning, simulation gives you scale, diversity, and precise labels. You can change the scene, the lighting, or the object arrangement, and generate situations that would be expensive to collect in the real world.

The harder part is interaction. When a robot grasps something, friction, contact, deformation, and small errors in control can matter a lot. A model can perform very well in simulation while exploiting details that don’t hold in reality. So I would judge simulation by whether it improves performance on real robots, rather than by how realistic it looks or how much data it produces.

My view is that simulation and real-world data should form a loop. Real-world failures tell you what your simulator is missing; simulation lets you explore those failures at scale; then you test the improvement in reality. The useful question is how much real-world learning you can gain for a given amount of time and cost.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation’s value depends on what the robot should learn and whether it improves real-robot performance, but does not state that value depends on data distribution rather than volume.

r002.rationale: It describes simulation as offering scale and diversity and generating varied scenes; it does not say simulation data can have a narrow, homogeneous distribution.

r003.rationale: It mentions friction, contact, deformation, and control errors, but does not identify limitations of current physics engines as an obstacle to simulating deformable-object interactions.

r004.rationale: It discusses learning gains relative to time and cost, but does not say real-robot data collection costs are declining for tasks that simulation already handles well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simulation data is very valuable, but its value depends on what you want the robot to learn. In simulation, you can generate a lot of interactions, control the conditions, and repeat failures without damaging hardware. That makes it useful for learning skills that would be expensive or difficult to collect in the real world.

The challenge is the gap between simulation and reality. A model can perform well in a simulator by relying on details that don’t hold in the physical world. Contact, friction, and deformable objects are particularly difficult. So I wouldn’t judge simulation data simply by its volume or how realistic it looks. I would ask: does training on it improve performance on a real robot?

My view is that simulation and real-world data should complement each other. Real-world experience can reveal where the simulator is wrong, and simulation can help expand coverage around those weaknesses. The goal is to make the data useful for transferring skills into the real world.
